strengths: The paper poses an interesting and timely question: whether generative image models contain transferable object-grouping structure that can be repurposed for category-agnostic instance segmentation.

The proposed instance-coloring objective is simple, intuitive, and reasonably well motivated, avoiding the need to impose arbitrary target colors while encouraging intra-instance consistency and inter-instance separation.

The empirical results are broad across several out-of-domain datasets, including art, egocentric images, irregular structures, and X-ray luggage, which supports the claim that the learned representations transfer beyond the narrow synthetic supervision set.

The comparison between Stable Diffusion and MAE variants is valuable because it suggests the effect is not solely due to internet-scale text-image pretraining; the MAE results make the core hypothesis more credible.
The paper includes useful ablations of the loss components and qualitative examples, and the appendix provides helpful implementation and dataset details.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that generative pretraining uniquely yields generalizable grouping is stronger than the evidence. The paper compares mainly against SimpleClick and a DINO-B+VAE construction, but does not include enough strong category-agnostic, self-supervised, open-vocabulary, or interactive segmentation baselines to isolate the role of generative pretraining.

The SimpleClick baseline performs extremely poorly despite using the same data and an MAE backbone, which raises concern about whether the baseline training/evaluation is properly matched or tuned. This result is important to the paper's argument and needs more validation.

The evaluation is mostly prompt-based with oracle ground-truth center points. This is useful, but it does not fully establish general-purpose instance segmentation performance in the standard detection/segmentation sense, such as AP, mask proposal quality, panoptic-style metrics, or performance without object-center prompts.

The comparison to SAM is informative but somewhat delicate: SAM is used as a high-water mark, yet the paper emphasizes selected cases where the proposed models outperform it, while the overall results still show large gaps for medium and small COCO objects and for some domains such as PIDRay and EgoHOS.

The training data is described as narrow, but Hypersim contains many unknown-category masks and millions of masks overall. Although SD-Limited helps, the exact leakage risk and semantic diversity of the supervision are not fully resolved.

The method has clear weaknesses on small objects, and these are central to many instance segmentation applications. The paper mostly attributes this to resolution and pretraining bias rather than demonstrating fixes or quantifying the tradeoff thoroughly.

Some claims about domains being unseen in pretraining, especially for Stable Diffusion and even MAE relative to broad ImageNet categories/styles, are hard to verify and should be stated more cautiously.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete in the manuscript itself: code and models are said to be available on a website, but the review cannot assess them from the paper, and several practical details of postprocessing/threshold sensitivity could use more analysis.

strengths: The paper explores an interesting direction: repurposing generative models, including Stable Diffusion and MAE encoder-decoder models, for category-agnostic instance segmentation via an instance-coloring objective.
The proposed loss is simple and reasonably motivated, encouraging intra-instance color consistency and inter-instance separation without requiring fixed color assignments.

The paper evaluates across several domain-shifted datasets, including COCO excluded categories, art, egocentric images, irregular structures, and X-ray imagery, which is a useful attempt to test generalization beyond the synthetic training categories.

The comparison between generative pretraining, discriminative DINO features, SimpleClick trained on the same data, and SAM provides some evidence that the generative decoder/representation may be useful for perceptual grouping.
The qualitative results on fine structures, especially iShape-like examples, are visually interesting and suggest a niche where the approach may capture boundaries that SAM sometimes misses.
weaknesses: The main claims are substantially overstated. The paper repeatedly suggests that generative models inherently learn general instance grouping, but the models are still fine-tuned with millions of supervised masks from synthetic datasets. This does not isolate an unsupervised or inherent capability of generative pretraining.

The quantitative evidence is not competitive with the strength of the claims. The best model only marginally exceeds SAM on COCOexc-L and iShape, while it is far worse on COCOexc-M/S, EgoHOS, and PIDRay, and below SAM on DRAM. Small-object performance is especially poor, e.g. 8.5 mIoU for SD on COCOexc-S versus 56.9 for SAM.

The evaluation protocol is narrow and favorable: most headline numbers use a single ground-truth center prompt. This does not demonstrate automatic instance segmentation quality, nor does it report standard AP/AR, mask proposal metrics, or full-scene instance segmentation performance.

The zero-shot framing is questionable. Stable Diffusion has internet-scale pretraining and may have seen many evaluation categories and styles; MAE pretraining on ImageNet includes many object categories. In addition, Hypersim has a very large 'unknown' category with instance masks, making it difficult to verify that evaluation categories are truly unseen during mask supervision.

The baselines are insufficient and sometimes not well matched. SimpleClick and DINO variants are trained/evaluated at 224x224 while SAM runs at much higher resolution; stronger category-agnostic or unsupervised segmentation/proposal methods, SAM2, Mask2Former-style models, CutLER-like approaches, or diffusion-feature segmentation methods are not thoroughly compared.

The paper’s strongest qualitative examples are explicitly selected to show cases where the proposed method beats SAM, and the random qualitative pages still show many blurry, merged, or incomplete masks. The visual evidence does not support the broad claim of near-SAM general-purpose segmentation.

The ablation study is weak: it is only reported on COCOexc with a single prompt and one model, with no statistical variation, no analysis across domains, and no ablation of important design choices such as thresholding, bilateral smoothing, prompt aggregation, training data composition, or resolution.

The edge detection experiment is only loosely connected to the main instance segmentation claim. Reporting that precision is better at low recall does not establish strong object boundary understanding, and the method misses many labeled boundaries at higher recall.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite a claimed website release. Important information such as exact train/validation splits, prompt sampling implementation, threshold sensitivity, compute for all variants, and failure-case statistics is either absent or too limited.

The paper would benefit from a more careful causal analysis. The observed improvements could stem from decoder architecture, resolution, synthetic training distribution, color-space objective, or post-processing choices rather than generative pretraining per se. Current experiments do not convincingly disentangle these factors.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and appealing idea: generative image models appear to encode transferable object grouping priors, and can be adapted to category-agnostic instance segmentation with limited synthetic mask supervision.

The proposed instance coloring loss is simple, well motivated, and broadly applicable across both Stable Diffusion and MAE encoder-decoder models, which strengthens the central hypothesis beyond a single architecture.
The empirical evaluation covers several meaningfully different out-of-distribution domains, including COCO excluded categories, artwork, egocentric scenes, irregular shapes, and X-ray imagery.

The comparison to SAM is ambitious and useful as a high-water mark, and the results are compelling on large objects and fine-structure datasets such as iShape, where the method can outperform SAM under the chosen prompting protocol.

The paper includes relevant diagnostic comparisons and ablations: MAE vs DINO, SimpleClick trained on the same data, SD-Limited, loss component ablations, multi-point prompting, and edge detection analysis.
The qualitative results are strong and help support the claim that the learned color embeddings capture perceptual grouping and compositional structure beyond the training categories.
weaknesses: The main evaluation relies on oracle prompt points, often at object centers, so the paper does not fully demonstrate general-purpose instance segmentation in the standard detection/proposal sense; it is closer to zero-shot promptable mask extraction from learned grouping features.

Performance remains substantially below SAM on many settings, especially medium and small COCO objects, EgoHOS, and PIDRay; the paper’s broad claims sometimes sound stronger than the quantitative evidence supports.

The comparison set is somewhat limited for a top-tier venue: stronger recent promptable segmentation systems, SAM2 variants, diffusion-feature segmentation methods, and other self-supervised/generative representation baselines would make the conclusions more robust.

The zero-shot framing is nuanced but still partly vulnerable to pretraining leakage or semantic exposure, especially for Stable Diffusion; the MAE results mitigate this concern, but the paper could separate pretraining exposure, mask-supervision exposure, and domain transfer more carefully.

The method’s practical pipeline is not fully satisfying: RGB color embeddings require thresholding, smoothing, and prompt-based querying, and the paper does not evaluate automatic mask generation quality, panoptic-style metrics, or downstream usability.
The computational and scalability aspects of the loss are under-discussed, especially with many instances per image, where the authors already cap the number of instances due to memory constraints.

Some claims about generative models uniquely learning transferable grouping are plausible but not fully established; DINO-B and SimpleClick may be disadvantaged by resolution, decoder choice, or training setup, so the causal attribution to generative pretraining remains somewhat incomplete.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting and timely question: whether generative pretraining induces transferable object grouping priors that can be exposed with limited mask supervision. The framing is clear and the empirical findings are potentially impactful for generalizable segmentation.

The method is simple and broadly applicable: representing instances as colors and fine-tuning generative decoders with an instance-coloring objective is easy to understand and can be applied to both MAE and Stable Diffusion backbones.

The evaluation covers several out-of-domain settings, including COCO excluded categories, art, egocentric data, irregular shapes, X-ray imagery, and BSDS500 edges. This gives meaningful evidence that the observed behavior is not confined to one benchmark.

The paper includes useful comparisons among generative and non-generative pretraining choices, including MAE, Stable Diffusion, DINO, SimpleClick, and SAM, which supports the core claim that generative pretraining is important.

Ablations on loss terms, training data diversity, number of supervised classes, timestep choice, color perturbations, and fine-tuning depth strengthen the empirical story and make the paper more convincing than a purely qualitative observation.
The qualitative results are compelling, especially for fine structures, ambiguous boundaries, and unusual domains where standard promptable segmentation models can struggle.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence. The results show useful transfer after supervised fine-tuning on 86k synthetic images and millions of masks, but do not fully establish that generative models learn an inherent general-purpose grouping mechanism rather than a useful inductive bias exposed by this particular training and prompting setup.

The evaluation is mostly point-prompted mIoU with ground-truth center prompts, not standard category-agnostic instance segmentation metrics such as mask AP, AR, PQ, or automatic proposal quality. This makes it hard to judge whether the method is competitive as an instance segmenter rather than as an interactive mask extractor under favorable prompts.

Performance is weak on small and medium COCO objects, and the paper acknowledges this but does not fully resolve it. This is an important limitation for practical instance segmentation and weakens the claim of broad general-purpose segmentation.

The edge-detection evaluation reports AP only under recall below 20%, justified by ambiguity, but this cherry-picks the part of the precision-recall curve where the method is strongest. Full-curve summary metrics would be needed to support the strong boundary-quality claims.

Some comparisons are not fully balanced. SAM is used as a high-water mark despite being optimized for different prompt protocols and resolutions, while the proposed models use low-dimensional color features and fixed thresholds. Stronger or more recent interactive/zero-shot segmentation baselines, SAM2 variants, learned decoders on the same features, and automatic mask generation comparisons would clarify the contribution.

The novelty of the loss is explicitly limited and related to prior discriminative embedding losses. The main contribution is therefore empirical, which is valuable, but the paper should be more careful in positioning the technical novelty.

The training data is described as narrow, but it still contains millions of masks and many indoor object types plus cars; additionally, Hypersim includes many unknown instance masks. The exact effect of unlabeled or ignored categories, unknown masks, and possible object overlap with evaluation categories deserves more rigorous treatment.

Reproducibility is decent in terms of hyperparameters, but the paper relies on a website for code/models and does not provide enough detail about threshold selection, bilateral filtering sensitivity, prompt handling, and dataset filtering to fully assess robustness from the manuscript alone.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting question: whether generative pretraining encodes transferable object grouping priors that can be adapted to category-agnostic instance segmentation with limited mask supervision.

The instance-coloring formulation is simple, architecture-agnostic, and easy to understand, and the authors are appropriately clear that the loss itself is inspired by prior discriminative embedding losses rather than wholly novel.

The empirical section covers several out-of-domain evaluation sets, including art, egocentric images, x-rays, fine-structure objects, and COCO categories excluded from the labeled training categories.
The paper includes useful ablations over loss terms, timestep choice, image perturbations, training data diversity, category restrictions, and depth of finetuning.
The qualitative results are visually engaging and suggest that generative backbones can indeed produce crisp boundaries and meaningful perceptual groupings in some challenging examples.
weaknesses: The main claim of strong zero-shot generalization is overstated. Stable Diffusion has internet-scale pretraining and may have seen many object categories and styles; the paper only excludes mask supervision, not visual exposure. The wording often blurs this distinction.

The training data story is concerning: Hypersim includes a very large 'unknown' category with instance annotations, and the paper does not clearly establish whether these unknown masks are used in the main training setup. If they are used, the claim that supervision is restricted to furnishings and cars is substantially weakened.

The comparison to SAM is not fully convincing. SAM is used as a high-water mark, but the promptable setup and postprocessing differ substantially, and the paper emphasizes selected regimes where the proposed model approaches or exceeds SAM while underplaying large gaps on medium/small COCO objects, EgoHOS, and PIDRay.

The baseline set is weak for supporting broad conclusions about generative versus discriminative pretraining. SimpleClick trained at 224x224 and a custom DINO+VAE baseline are not sufficient to rule out stronger discriminative, self-supervised, promptable, or modern segmentation baselines under matched resolution and training conditions.

The edge detection evaluation is particularly fragile: reporting AP only below 20% recall is a cherry-picked metric justified post hoc by model behavior. This does not support the broad claim that the method outperforms SAM on boundaries in a general sense.

The method depends on hand-designed thresholding, bilateral smoothing, and RGB color embedding heuristics, yet sensitivity to these prompt-time choices is not sufficiently explored. The reported fixed threshold may not transfer reliably across datasets and models.

The paper repeatedly makes broad interpretive claims about 'inherent grouping mechanisms' in generative models, but the evidence is correlational. Alternative explanations such as training-set leakage through unknown masks, resolution effects, VAE/decoder priors, dataset biases, and postprocessing choices are not adequately ruled out.

The evaluation is missing stronger reproducibility details and practical metrics for instance segmentation quality beyond center-point IoU, such as AP-style instance metrics, failure rates, object-size-stratified analysis beyond COCO, and comparisons under consistent multi-point prompting protocols.

Some qualitative figures are persuasive but risk cherry-picking despite a few 'randomly chosen' captions; the strongest claims rely too much on visual examples rather than rigorous aggregate analysis.
Overall, the paper has an interesting direction, but the novelty is modest and the experimental evidence does not support the strength of the claims at a top-tier AI conference acceptance bar.

strengths: The paper asks a compelling and well-motivated question: whether generative pretraining induces transferable object grouping mechanisms that can be repurposed for category-agnostic instance segmentation under narrow mask supervision.

The empirical results are interesting and often surprising. Fine-tuned Stable Diffusion and MAE models generalize from synthetic furnishings/cars to COCO-excluded categories, art, egocentric images, fine structures, and X-ray imagery, with particularly strong performance on large objects and iShape.

The comparison between generative models, DINO, SimpleClick, and SAM is informative. The poor performance of SimpleClick trained on the same data and the stronger MAE/SD results provide concrete evidence that the effect is not simply due to synthetic training masks.

The paper includes useful ablations over training data diversity, loss components, timestep choice, color perturbations, and fine-tuning depth. These strengthen the central claim that pretrained generative decoders carry useful grouping information.
The method is simple and broadly applicable: representing instance segmentation as image-to-image prediction with an instance-coloring loss is easy to understand and appears architecture-agnostic.
The qualitative results are extensive and help illustrate strengths on fine boundaries, compositional parts, and unusual visual domains.
weaknesses: The central explanation that generative pretraining learns an inherent grouping mechanism is plausible but still somewhat overclaimed. The experiments show strong transfer after supervised fine-tuning, but do not fully isolate whether the gains arise from generative objectives, decoder architecture, pretraining data scale, output resolution, or other architectural biases.

The comparison to SAM is useful but not always fair or complete. SAM is optimized for promptable segmentation with different training data and objectives, while the proposed method uses oracle center prompts and a custom thresholding/similarity procedure. Claims about approaching or outperforming SAM should be framed more carefully, especially since performance is much worse on medium and small COCO objects and on PIDRay/EgoHOS.

Evaluation is broad but still incomplete for a top-tier claim. The paper would benefit from stronger baselines such as SAM2, HQ-SAM or other high-quality interactive segmentation variants, diffusion-feature segmentation methods, unsupervised object discovery methods, and stronger discriminative dense-feature baselines beyond DINO-B+VAE.

The zero-shot framing is partially ambiguous. Stable Diffusion has internet-scale pretraining and MAE/ImageNet pretraining includes many object categories, so the models may have seen the visual categories, even if not their masks. The paper is careful in places about unseen masks, but some broader language suggests stronger novelty than the setting supports.

The proposed instance-coloring loss is explicitly not very novel and resembles prior discriminative embedding losses. The main contribution is therefore empirical and conceptual; this is valuable, but the paper should be clearer that the algorithmic novelty is limited.

Small-object segmentation is a clear weakness: COCO medium/small results are far below SAM, and the paper mostly explains this post hoc. For a general-purpose instance segmentation claim, this limitation is significant.

Some evaluation choices need more justification. Reporting BSDS edge AP only below 20% recall favors precision on selected object boundaries and may understate missed-object failures; full-curve metrics should be emphasized more prominently.

Reproducibility is promising but not fully established from the manuscript alone. The paper mentions code/models/demos on a website, but the review would be stronger with clearer implementation details for the prompt thresholding, data filtering, category exclusions, and exact evaluation protocol in the main text.
